questions.question_text: A wafer of pure germanium crystal has two parts X and Y. The end X is obtained by doping with arsenic and Y with indium. It is connected to a battery as shown in the figure. Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.question_html: A wafer of pure germanium crystal has two parts X and Y. The end X is obtained by doping with arsenic and Y with indium. It is connected to a battery as shown in the figure. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: X is p-type, Y is n-type and the junction is forward biased
options.html: X is p-type, Y is n-type and the junction is forward biased

options.label: B
options.text: X is n-type, Y is p-type and the junction is forward biased
options.html: X is n-type, Y is p-type and the junction is forward biased

options.label: C
options.text: X is p-type, Y is n-type and the junction is reverse biased
options.html: X is p-type, Y is n-type and the junction is reverse biased

options.label: D
options.text: X is n-type, Y is p-type and the junction is reverse biased
options.html: X is n-type, Y is p-type and the junction is reverse biased

questions.explanation_text: Part X is doped with arsenic. Arsenic is a Group 15 element, so it has 5 valence electrons. When it is added to germanium, it gives extra free electrons. So, part X becomes an n-type semiconductor. Part Y is doped with indium. Indium is a Group 13 element, so it has 3 valence electrons. When it is added to germanium, it creates holes. So, part Y becomes a p-type semiconductor. In the battery symbol, the longer line represents the positive terminal, and the shorter line represents the negative terminal. From the figure, part X is connected to the positive terminal and part Y is connected to the negative terminal. Since the n-type side is connected to the positive terminal and the p-type side is connected to the negative terminal, the p-n junction is reverse biased.
questions.explanation_html:
Part X is doped with arsenic. Arsenic is a Group 15 element, so it has 5 valence electrons. When it is added to germanium, it gives extra free electrons. So, part X becomes an n-type semiconductor.

Part Y is doped with indium. Indium is a Group 13 element, so it has 3 valence electrons. When it is added to germanium, it creates holes. So, part Y becomes a p-type semiconductor.

In the battery symbol, the longer line represents the positive terminal, and the shorter line represents the negative terminal.

From the figure, part X is connected to the positive terminal and part Y is connected to the negative terminal.

Since the n-type side is connected to the positive terminal and the p-type side is connected to the negative terminal, the p-n junction is reverse biased.

questions.question_html: In which of the following figures, diode is reverse biased?

options.label: A

questions.explanation_text: A diode is reverse biased when its p-side, called the anode, is at a lower potential than its n-side, called the cathode. So, the condition for reverse bias is: $V_{p}<V_{n}$ Now check each option. For option (A): $V_{p}=5\text{V}$ and $V_{n}=0\text{V}$ (grounded). Here, $V_{p}>V_{n}$ . So, the diode is forward biased. For option (B): $V_{p}=-20\text{V}$ and $V_{n}=-10\text{V}$ . Here, $V_{p}<V_{n}$ because $-20\text{V}<-10\text{V}$ . So, the diode is reverse biased. For option (C): $V_{p}=15\text{V}$ and $V_{n}=10\text{V}$ . Here, $V_{p}>V_{n}$ . So, the diode is forward biased. For option (D): $V_{p}=20\text{V}$ and $V_{n}=-5\text{V}$ . Here, $V_{p}>V_{n}$ . So, the diode is forward biased. Thus, the diode in option (B) is reverse biased.
questions.explanation_html:
A diode is reverse biased when its p-side, called the anode, is at a lower potential than its n-side, called the cathode.

So, the condition for reverse bias is:

$V_{p}<V_{n}$

Now check each option.

For option (A):

$V_{p}=5\text{V}$ and $V_{n}=0\text{V}$ (grounded).

Here, $V_{p}>V_{n}$ . So, the diode is forward biased.

For option (B):

$V_{p}=-20\text{V}$ and $V_{n}=-10\text{V}$ .

Here, $V_{p}<V_{n}$ because $-20\text{V}<-10\text{V}$ .

So, the diode is reverse biased.

For option (C):

$V_{p}=15\text{V}$ and $V_{n}=10\text{V}$ .

Here, $V_{p}>V_{n}$ . So, the diode is forward biased.

For option (D):

$V_{p}=20\text{V}$ and $V_{n}=-5\text{V}$ .

Here, $V_{p}>V_{n}$ . So, the diode is forward biased.

Thus, the diode in option (B) is reverse biased.

questions.explanation_text: An $n$ -type semiconductor is obtained by doping pure silicon with a pentavalent impurity, such as Phosphorus or Arsenic. A $p$ -type semiconductor is obtained by doping pure silicon with a trivalent impurity, such as Boron, Aluminium, or Indium. So, for silicon: $n\text{-type} \rightarrow \text{Phosphorus}$ $p\text{-type} \rightarrow \text{Indium}$ Hence, the correct option is: $\text{Option C: Phosphorous and Indium respectively}$
questions.explanation_html:
An $n$ -type semiconductor is obtained by doping pure silicon with a pentavalent impurity, such as Phosphorus or Arsenic.

A $p$ -type semiconductor is obtained by doping pure silicon with a trivalent impurity, such as Boron, Aluminium, or Indium.

So, for silicon:

$n\text{-type} \rightarrow \text{Phosphorus}$

$p\text{-type} \rightarrow \text{Indium}$

Hence, the correct option is:

$\text{Option C: Phosphorous and Indium respectively}$

questions.question_text: The density of electron-hole pair in a pure germanium is $3 \times 10^{16}m^{-3}$ at room temperature. On doping with aluminium, the hole density increases to $4.5 \times 10^{22}m^{-3}$ . Now, the electron density (in $m^{-3}$ ) in doped germanium will be
questions.question_html: The density of electron-hole pair in a pure germanium is $3 \times 10^{16}m^{-3}$ at room temperature. On doping with aluminium, the hole density increases to $4.5 \times 10^{22}m^{-3}$ . Now, the electron density (in $m^{-3}$ ) in doped germanium will be
questions.explanation_text: When germanium is pure (intrinsic), the electron density $n_{i}$ and the hole density $p_{i}$ are equal and given as: $n_{i}=p_{i}=3 \times 10^{16}\text{m}^{-3}.$ After doping with aluminium (which is an acceptor impurity), the hole density increases to: $p=4.5 \times 10^{22}\text{m}^{-3}.$ In a semiconductor, the law of mass action holds, which states that: $n \times p=n_{i}^{2},$ where $n$ is the electron density in the doped semiconductor. To find $n$ (the electron density in doped germanium), follow these steps: Calculate the square of the intrinsic carrier concentration: $n_{i}^{2}=(3 \times 10^{16})^{2}=9 \times 10^{32}\text{m}^{-6}.$ Use the mass action law to solve for $n$ : $n=\frac{n_{i}^{2}}{p}=\frac{9 \times 10^{32}}{4.5 \times 10^{22}}.$ Perform the division: $n=2 \times 10^{10}\text{m}^{-3}.$ Thus, the electron density in the doped germanium is $2 \times 10^{10}\text{m}^{-3},$ which corresponds to Option B.
questions.explanation_html:
When germanium is pure (intrinsic), the electron density $n_{i}$ and the hole density $p_{i}$ are equal and given as:

$n_{i}=p_{i}=3 \times 10^{16}\text{m}^{-3}.$

After doping with aluminium (which is an acceptor impurity), the hole density increases to:

$p=4.5 \times 10^{22}\text{m}^{-3}.$

In a semiconductor, the law of mass action holds, which states that:

$n \times p=n_{i}^{2},$

where $n$ is the electron density in the doped semiconductor.

To find $n$ (the electron density in doped germanium), follow these steps:

Calculate the square of the intrinsic carrier concentration:

$n_{i}^{2}=(3 \times 10^{16})^{2}=9 \times 10^{32}\text{m}^{-6}.$

Use the mass action law to solve for $n$ :

$n=\frac{n_{i}^{2}}{p}=\frac{9 \times 10^{32}}{4.5 \times 10^{22}}.$

Perform the division:

$n=2 \times 10^{10}\text{m}^{-3}.$

Thus, the electron density in the doped germanium is $2 \times 10^{10}\text{m}^{-3},$ which corresponds to Option B.

The potential difference applied across the collector and emitter of a transistor used in CE configuration is, $V_{CE}=2V$ . If the collector resistance $R_{C}=4k\Omega$ , the base current $(I_{B})$ and the collector current $(I_{C})$ are
questions.question_html: The DC common emitter current gain of an $n-p-n$ transistor is 50 . The potential difference applied across the collector and emitter of a transistor used in CE configuration is, $V_{CE}=2V$ . If the collector resistance $R_{C}=4k\Omega$ , the base current $(I_{B})$ and the collector current $(I_{C})$ are
questions.explanation_text: Let's analyze the problem step by step. We are given the DC current gain of the common emitter (CE) configuration: $\beta=\frac{I_{C}}{I_{B}}=50.$ This means that the collector current is 50 times the base current: $I_{C}=50I_{B}.$ The circuit has a collector resistor: $R_{C}=4k\Omega,$ and the voltage applied across the collector and emitter is: $V_{CE}=2V.$ In a common emitter configuration, the supply voltage (say, $V_{CC}$ ) is shared between the collector resistor and the transistor. That is, $V_{CC}=I_{C}R_{C}+V_{CE}.$ Although $V_{CC}$ is not given explicitly, we can use the available values to find a consistent solution. Suppose the voltage drop across $R_{C}$ is equal to: $V_{R_{C}}=I_{C}R_{C}.$ For a consistent operating point, one possible scenario is that: $V_{R_{C}}=2V.$ Then, $I_{C}R_{C}=2V⟹I_{C}=\frac{2V}{4k\Omega}=0.5mA.$ Now, using the relation $I_{B}=\frac{I_{C}}{\beta},$ we get: $I_{B}=\frac{0.5mA}{50}=0.01mA=10\mu A.$ Thus, we have: Base Current, $I_{B}=10\mu A$ Collector Current, $I_{C}=0.5mA$ These results correspond to Option A.
questions.explanation_html:
Let's analyze the problem step by step.

We are given the DC current gain of the common emitter (CE) configuration:

$\beta=\frac{I_{C}}{I_{B}}=50.$

This means that the collector current is 50 times the base current:

$I_{C}=50I_{B}.$

The circuit has a collector resistor:

$R_{C}=4k\Omega,$

and the voltage applied across the collector and emitter is:

$V_{CE}=2V.$

In a common emitter configuration, the supply voltage (say, $V_{CC}$ ) is shared between the collector resistor and the transistor. That is,

$V_{CC}=I_{C}R_{C}+V_{CE}.$

Although $V_{CC}$ is not given explicitly, we can use the available values to find a consistent solution.

Suppose the voltage drop across $R_{C}$ is equal to:

$V_{R_{C}}=I_{C}R_{C}.$

For a consistent operating point, one possible scenario is that:

$V_{R_{C}}=2V.$

Then,

$I_{C}R_{C}=2V⟹I_{C}=\frac{2V}{4k\Omega}=0.5mA.$

Now, using the relation

$I_{B}=\frac{I_{C}}{\beta},$

we get:

$I_{B}=\frac{0.5mA}{50}=0.01mA=10\mu A.$

Thus, we have:

Base Current, $I_{B}=10\mu A$

Collector Current, $I_{C}=0.5mA$

These results correspond to Option A.

questions.question_text: The energy gap in case of which of the following is less than 3 eV ?
questions.question_html: The energy gap in case of which of the following is less than 3 eV ?
questions.explanation_text: The energy gap (or band gap) is the energy difference between the valence band and the conduction band in a material. Semiconductors have a finite band gap that allows electrons to jump from the valence band to the conduction band with the absorption of energy. Typically, the band gap in semiconductors is less than 3 eV. For example, Germanium has a band gap of around $0.66\text{eV}$ . Metals, on the other hand, have overlapping conduction and valence bands, meaning they do not have a meaningful band gap (effectively, the gap is 0 eV). Given the options: Option A: Germanium (a semiconductor with $∼0.66\text{eV}$ band gap, which is less than 3 eV) Options B (Iron), C (Copper), and D (Aluminium) are metals and do not exhibit a band gap in the context of semiconductor physics. Thus, the correct answer is: Option A Germanium

questions.question_text: Which of the following semi-conducting device is used as voltage regulator?
questions.question_html: Which of the following semi-conducting device is used as voltage regulator?

options.label: A
options.html: LASER diode

options.label: D
options.html: Photo diode

questions.explanation_text: The correct answer is Option B: Zener diode. Here’s why: A voltage regulator maintains a constant voltage level regardless of changes in the load current or supply voltage. A Zener diode, when reverse-biased, enters a breakdown region at its specified Zener voltage. In this region, it maintains approximately that voltage across its terminals even if the current varies. This characteristic makes the Zener diode ideal for use in simple voltage regulation circuits. The other options do not serve this function: A laser diode is primarily used for emitting focused light in optical applications. A solar cell converts light energy into electrical energy. A photodiode detects light and converts it into a current but does not regulate voltage. Thus, the Zener diode is the semiconductor device used as a voltage regulator.
